claim: 25 participants (19–31 years, mean age 24.6 years, ±3.5 years SD; 10 male) with self-reported normal hearing took part in the experiment.
source: 25 participants (19–31 years, mean age 24.6 years,±3.5 years SD; 10 male) with self-reported normal hearing took part in the experiment.
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics in the manuscript.

claim: Participants gave written informed consent and were financially compensated.
source: Participants gave written informed consent and were financially compensated.
evidence: Direct statement about consent and compensation procedures.

claim: None of the participants reported a history of neurological or otological disease.
source: None of the participants reported a history of neurological or otological disease.
evidence: Direct statement about participant health status.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committee of the University of Lübeck.
source: The study was approved by the local ethics committee of the University of Lübeck and all experimental procedures were carried out in accordance with the registered protocol.
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Stimuli were presented via air conducting in-ear head phones (EARTONE 3A), Psychtoolbox and a low latency audio card (RME Audio).
source: Stimuli were presented via air conducting in-ear head phones (EARTONE 3A), Psychtoolbox and a low latency audio card (RME Audio).
evidence: Direct statement about equipment used for stimulus presentation.

claim: All stimuli were presented perfectly audible at a comfortable loudness level approximating 60 dB SPL.
source: All stimuli were presented perfectly audible at a comfortable loudness level approximating 60 dB SPL.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus presentation parameters.

claim: Participants performed 60 trials per stimulus level, resulting in 420 trials split up into 10 blocks of 42 trials each.
source: Participants performed 60 trials per stimulus levels, resulting in 420 trials split up into 10 blocks of 42 trials each.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design.

claim: The average tone-to-tone interval varied between individuals (9.14 ± 1.04 s; min = 8.28 s, max = 12.32 s).
source: Note that since the exact time point of stimulus presentation was determined depending on current brain states as identified by the real-time approach outlined below, the average tone-to-tone interval varied between individuals (9.14 ± 1.04 s; min = 8.28 s, max = 12.32 s).
evidence: Direct statement with measured values.

claim: EEG signals were measured with a 64-channel active electrode system (actichamp, BrainProducts, Germany).
source: While participants were seated in a dimly lit, sound attenuated booth, EEG signals were measured with a 64-channel active electrode system (actichamp, BrainProducts, Germany).
evidence: Direct statement about EEG recording equipment.

claim: Electrodes were arranged according to the international 10–20 system and impedances were kept below 10 kΩ.
source: Electrodes were arranged according to the international 10–20 system and impedances were kept below 10 kΩ.
evidence: Direct statement about electrode placement and impedance criteria.

claim: EEG data were sampled at 1 kHz and referenced to electrode TP9 (left mastoid).
source: Data were sampled at 1 kHz, referenced to electrode TP9 (left mastoid), and recorded using Labrecorder software, part of the Lab Streaming Layer (LSL; Kothe, 2014), also used to create a stream of EEG data, accessible in real-time.
evidence: Direct statement about EEG recording parameters.

claim: Pupil size was recorded by tracking participants' right eye at 500 Hz (Eyelink 1000, SR Research).
source: Additionally, eye blinks were monitored and pupil size was recorded by tracking participants' right eye at 500 Hz (Eyelink 1000, SR Research).
evidence: Direct statement about pupillometry recording.

claim: A spatial filter was calculated based on the data from the auditory localizer task of each participant excluding oddball trials.
source: To focus on EEG activity from auditory cortices, a spatial filter was calculated based on the data from the auditory localizer task of each participant excluding oddball trials.
evidence: Direct statement about spatial filtering procedure.

claim: Singular value decomposition was applied based on the difference between a signal covariance matrix (estimated on EEG data from 0 to 200 ms peristimulus) and a noise covariance matrix (−200–0 ms peristimulus).
source: After re-referencing to the average off all channels, we applied singular value decomposition based on the difference between a signal covariance matrix (estimated on EEG data from 0 to 200 ms peristimulus) and a noise covariance matrix (−200–0 ms peristimulus).
evidence: Direct statement about signal processing method.

claim: The elements of the first eigenvector were used as filter weights.
source: This approach resulted in a 64 × 64 matrix of eigenvalues and the elements of the first eigenvector were used as filter weights (for similar approaches see de Cheveigné and Simon, 2008; Herrmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement about filter weight calculation with citations to similar approaches.

claim: Matrix multiplication of incoming EEG signals with the spatial filter weights resulted in one virtual EEG channel which largely reflected activity from auditory cortical regions.
source: Matrix multiplication of incoming EEG signals with the spatial filter weights resulted in one virtual EEG channel which largely reflected activity from auditory cortical regions.
evidence: Direct statement about the result of spatial filtering.

claim: Source projection of localizer data revealed predominantly auditory cortical regions as generators.
source: Source projection of localizer data which were used to construct the subject-specific spatial filters revealed predominantly auditory cortical regions as generators (Figure 2a).
evidence: Statement supported by source localization analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Weighted permutation entropy (WPE) was computed of spatially filtered EEG-signals in a moving window fashion.
source: We computed weighted permutation entropy (WPE) of spatially filtered EEG-signals in a moving window fashion.
evidence: Direct statement about entropy calculation method.

claim: WPE is an extension to permutation entropy (PE) which was first developed by Bandt and Pompe (2002) that considers the amplitude fluctuations of time-series data.
source: WPE is an extension to permutation entropy (PE) which was first developed by Bandt and Pompe (2002) that considers the amplitude fluctuations of time-series data (Fadlallah et al., 2013) and its calculation is outlined below.
evidence: Direct statement with citations to original methods.

claim: A 200-samples window was moved along the EEG signal in steps of 10 samples, resulting in an entropy sampling rate of 100 Hz.
source: To ensure approximation acuity but to retain a high time-resolution, a 200-samples window was moved along the EEG signal in steps of 10 samples, resulting in an entropy sampling rate of 100 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement about entropy calculation parameters.

claim: The entropy distribution was updated constantly such that it never depended on values older than 30 s.
source: Importantly, this distribution was updated constantly such that it never depended on values older than 30 s.
evidence: Direct statement about the real-time algorithm's updating procedure.

claim: Desynchronization states were defined as a minimum of 10 consecutive entropy samples (100 ms) higher or lower than 90% of the current distribution.
source: Desynchronization states were defined as a minimum of 10 consecutive entropy samples (100 ms) higher or lower than 90% of the current distribution.
evidence: Direct statement about state detection criteria.

claim: Whenever a blink was detected by the eye tracker or pupil size was close to zero, a 'mute' window of 1 s was initiated where incoming EEG data were not considered further.
source: To this end, pupil data was read out in real-time and whenever a blink was detected by the eye tracker or pupil size was close to zero, a 'mute' window of 1 s was initiated where incoming EEG data were not considered further.
evidence: Direct statement about artifact rejection procedure.

claim: Each tone was presented equally often during high and low states (30 times, yielding 210 trials per state, or 420 trials in total).
source: Note that each tone was presented equally often during high and low states (30 times, yielding 210 trials per state, or 420 trials in total).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design balance.

claim: Signal around blinks was interpolated using a cubic spline before low-pass filtering below 20 Hz and down-sampling to 50 Hz.
source: Second, signal around blinks was interpolated using a cubic spline before low-pass filtering below 20 Hz and down-sampling to 50 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement about pupil data preprocessing.

claim: Single trial time-courses of pupil size were visually inspected and noisy trials (1.3 ± 1.6%) were removed.
source: Finally, single trial time-courses of pupil size were visually inspected and noisy trials (1.3 ± 1.6%) were removed.
evidence: Direct statement about data quality control with percentage of rejected trials.

claim: Due to technical difficulties, data from one subject had to be excluded from pupillometry analyses.
source: Due to technical difficulties, data from one subject had to be excluded from further analyses.
evidence: Direct statement about data exclusion.

claim: On average one channel (±1 channel, M ± SD), 68.9% (±7%) of all components, and 1.4% (±1.6%) of all trials were rejected during EEG preprocessing.
source: On average one channel (±1 channel, M ± SD), 68.9% (±7%) of all components, and 1.4% (±1.6%) of all trials were rejected.
evidence: Direct statement about EEG data rejection rates.

claim: Single trial complex-valued Fourier representations of the data were obtained through the convolution of cleaned and spatially filtered time-courses with frequency adaptive Hann-tapers (four cycles) with a time-resolution of 100 Hz.
source: Single trial complex-valued Fourier representations of the data were obtained through the convolution of cleaned and spatially filtered time-courses with frequency adaptive Hann-tapers (four cycles) with a time-resolution of 100 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement about time-frequency analysis method.

claim: Power from 1 to 40 Hz (in .5 Hz steps) and from 40 to 70 Hz (14 exponentially increasing steps) was calculated by squaring the modulus of the Fourier spectrum.
source: Power from 1 to 40 Hz (in. 5 Hz steps) and from 40 to 70 Hz (14 exponentially increasing steps) was calculated by squaring the modulus of the Fourier spectrum and was expressed as change in Decibel (dB) relative to average power in the whole trial (−1 to 1.5 s peristimulus).
evidence: Direct statement about power calculation method.

claim: Inter-trial phase coherence (ITC) was calculated by dividing Fourier representations by their magnitude and averaging across trials before computing the magnitude of the average complex value.
source: Additionally, we calculated inter-trial phase coherence (ITC; 0 ≤ ITC ≥ 1) and thus divided Fourier representations by their magnitude and averaged across trials before computing the magnitude of the average complex value.
evidence: Direct statement about ITC calculation method.

claim: Single-trial phase coherence was computed using jackknife-ITC (jITC), where jITC of one trial is defined as the ITC of all trials but the one in question.
source: Importantly, since, ITC is only defined for a set of multiple trials but not for single trials, we computed the single-trial measure of jackknife-ITC (jITC; Richter et al., 2015; Wöstmann et al., 2019). In short, jITC of one trial is defined as the ITC of all trials but the one in question.
evidence: Direct statement about single-trial phase coherence calculation with citations.

claim: Average entropy time-courses were elevated for all classified-high compared to all classified-low states in a 200 ms pre-stimulus window (all p<0.001, FDR corrected).
source: Demonstrating the performance of the real-time algorithm, average entropy time-courses were elevated for all classified-high compared to all classified-low states in a 200 ms pre-stimulus window (all p<0.001, FDR corrected; Figure 2b).
evidence: Statistical result with p-values and reference to figure.

claim: Pupil diameter time-courses did not differ between high and low entropy states at any point in time (all p>0.1).
source: In contrast, pupil diameter time-courses did not differ between high and low entropy states at any point in time (all p>0.1) nor did the distributions of pre-stimulus pupil diameters (Figure 2c).
evidence: Statistical result with p-values and reference to figure.

claim: Pupil size and entropy in the pre-stimulus time window were positively related (β = 0.02, SE = 0.01, p=0.02).
source: In line with previous research (Reimer et al., 2014), pupil size and entropy in the pre-stimulus time window were positively related (β = 0.02, SE = 0.01, p=0.02).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus citation to previous research.

claim: Pupil size explained less than 1% of the variance in EEG entropy.
source: Pupil size explained less than 1% of the variance in EEG entropy.
evidence: Direct statement about variance explained.

claim: EEG entropy states were self-similar on an approximate ~500 ms scale, while states of pupil size extended over several seconds.
source: Furthermore, auditory cortical desynchronization and pupil linked arousal, as approximated by EEG entropy and pupil size, displayed different autocorrelation functions (Figure 2b). While EEG entropy states were self-similar on an approximate ~500 ms scale, states of pupil size extended over several seconds.
evidence: Statement about autocorrelation analysis with reference to figure.

claim: Pre-stimulus entropy displayed a negative relationship with oscillatory power within the pre-stimulus time window (−200–0 ms).
source: As expected based on the definition of entropy and earlier results (Waschke et al., 2017), these analyses revealed a negative relationship of entropy and oscillatory power within the pre-stimulus time window (−200–0 ms; Figure 3).
evidence: Statement about analysis results with citation and figure reference.

claim: With increasing pre-stimulus entropy, low-frequency pre-stimulus power decreased (1–8 Hz, linear: β = −0.18, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; quadratic: β = 0.03, SE = 0.009, p<.005).
source: With increasing pre-stimulus entropy, low-frequency pre-stimulus power decreased (1–8 Hz, linear: β = −0.18, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; quadratic: β = 0.03, SE = 0.009, p<.005; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Statistical results with effect sizes, standard errors, and p-values.

claim: Gamma power (40–70 Hz) decreased with increasing pre-stimulus entropy (linear: β = −0.18, SE = 0.01, p<0.001).
source: Gamma power (40–70 Hz) also decreased (linear: β = −0.18, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value.

claim: Gamma power was lowest at intermediate entropy levels (quadratic effect; β = 0.06, SE = 0.009, p<0.001).
source: Gamma power was lowest at intermediate entropy levels (quadratic effect; β = 0.06, SE = 0.009, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value.

claim: EEG entropy was negatively related to pre-stimulus alpha power (8–12 Hz, β = −0.29, SE = 0.01, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, EEG entropy was negatively related to pre-stimulus alpha power (8–12 Hz, β = −0.29, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 & Supplementary file 2) and beta power (14–30 Hz, β = −0.32, SE = 0.01, p<0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 & Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Statistical results with effect sizes, standard errors, and p-values, plus figure references.

claim: EEG entropy was negatively related to pre-stimulus beta power (14–30 Hz, β = −0.32, SE = 0.01, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, EEG entropy was negatively related to pre-stimulus alpha power (8–12 Hz, β = −0.29, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 & Supplementary file 2) and beta power (14–30 Hz, β = −0.32, SE = 0.01, p<0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 & Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Statistical results with effect sizes, standard errors, and p-values, plus figure references.

claim: Pupil size was associated with a decrease in pre-stimulus low-frequency power (1–8 Hz, linear: β = −0.04, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; quadratic: β = 0.016, SE = 0.006, p<0.05).
source: Analogously, pupil size was associated with a decrease in pre-stimulus low-frequency power (1–8 Hz, linear: β = −0.04, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; quadratic: β = 0.016, SE = 0.006, p<0.05; Supplementary file 1) but did not display a substantial relationship with gamma power (all p>0.2 see Figure 3; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Statistical results with effect sizes, standard errors, and p-values, plus figure references.

claim: Pupil size did not display a substantial relationship with gamma power (all p>0.2).
source: Analogously, pupil size was associated with a decrease in pre-stimulus low-frequency power (1–8 Hz, linear: β = −0.04, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; quadratic: β = 0.016, SE = 0.006, p<0.05; Supplementary file 1) but did not display a substantial relationship with gamma power (all p>0.2 see Figure 3; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Statistical result with p-values and figure reference.

claim: Pupil size was positively related with pre-stimulus beta power (14–30 Hz, β = 0.04, SE = 0.01, p<0.001).
source: Notably, pupil size was positively related with pre-stimulus beta power (14–30 Hz, β = 0.04, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3) but not with alpha power (all p>0.3).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus figure reference.

claim: Pupil size was not related with alpha power (all p>0.3).
source: Notably, pupil size was positively related with pre-stimulus beta power (14–30 Hz, β = 0.04, SE = 0.01, p<0.001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3) but not with alpha power (all p>0.3).
evidence: Statistical result with p-values.

claim: The stronger negative linear link of EEG entropy with low-frequency power compared to pupil size was supported by the Wald test (ZWald = 9.1, p<0.001).
source: The stronger negative linear link of EEG entropy with low-frequency power compared to pupil size was supported by the Wald test (ZWald = 9.1, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison result with test statistic and p-value.

claim: Low-frequency single-trial phase coherence after stimulus onset increased with pre-stimulus entropy (1–8 Hz, 0–400 ms; β = 0.05, SE = 0.01, p<0.001).
source: First, we found low-frequency single-trial phase coherence after stimulus onset, a measure quantifying the consistency of phase-locked responses on a trial-wise basis (see Materials and methods for details), to increase with pre-stimulus entropy (1–8 Hz, 0–400 ms; β = 0.05, SE = 0.01, p<0.001, Figure 4a,d).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus figure references.

claim: Phase coherence saturated at intermediate levels of pre-stimulus entropy, as evidenced by a negative quadratic effect (β = −0.02 SE=0.009, p=0.02).
source: Additionally, phase coherence did not only increase with pre-stimulus entropy but saturated at intermediate levels, as evidenced by a negative quadratic effect (β = −0.02 SE=0.009, p=0.02, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value.

claim: There was no comparable relationship of pupil size and single-trial phase coherence (1–jITC; β = −0.005, SE = 0.006, p=0.5; ZWald = 1.5, p=0.1).
source: Of note, there was no comparable relationship of pupil size and single-trial phase coherence (1–jITC, see Materials and methods for details; β = −0.005, SE = 0.006, p=0.5; ZWald = 1.5, p=0.1).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-values.

claim: Low-frequency power after stimulus onset decreased linearly as a function of pre-stimulus entropy (1–8 Hz, 0–400 ms; β = −0.02, SE = 0.01, p=0.017).
source: Second, we observed a linear decrease of low-frequency power after stimulus onset, as a function of pre-stimulus entropy (1–8 Hz, 0–400 ms; β = −0.02, SE = 0.01, p=0.017, Figure 4b,e).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus figure references.

claim: Pre-stimulus pupil size did not affect post-stimulus low-frequency power significantly (β = 0.015, SE = 0.011, p=0.2).
source: In contrast, pre-stimulus pupil size did not affect post-stimulus low-frequency power significantly (β = 0.015, SE = 0.011, p=0.2; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value.

claim: Stimulus-induced activity in low frequencies changed linearly with auditory cortical desynchronization but remained unaltered under changing levels of pupil-linked arousal (ZWald = 2.6, p=0.009).
source: Therefore, stimulus-induced activity in low frequencies changed linearly with auditory cortical desynchronization but remained unaltered under changing levels of pupil-linked arousal (ZWald = 2.6, p=0.009).
evidence: Statistical comparison result with test statistic and p-value.

claim: Post-stimulus oscillatory power in the alpha band increased linearly with pupil linked arousal (β = 0.033, SE = 0.01, p<.005).
source: Notably, post-stimulus oscillatory power in the alpha band increased linearly with pupil linked arousal (β = 0.033, SE = 0.01, p<.005; Figure 4—figure supplement 2 & Supplementary file 6) but not with auditory cortical desynchronization (β = −0.008, SE = 0.009, p=0.5).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus figure reference.

claim: Post-stimulus oscillatory power in the alpha band did not increase with auditory cortical desynchronization (β = −0.008, SE = 0.009, p=0.5).
source: Notably, post-stimulus oscillatory power in the alpha band increased linearly with pupil linked arousal (β = 0.033, SE = 0.01, p<.005; Figure 4—figure supplement 2 & Supplementary file 6) but not with auditory cortical desynchronization (β = −0.008, SE = 0.009, p=0.5).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value.

claim: Oscillatory power in the beta band was neither substantially linked to pre-stimulus auditory cortical desynchronization nor pupil-linked arousal (all p>0.2).
source: Oscillatory power in the beta band was neither substantially linked to pre-stimulus auditory cortical desynchronization nor pupil-linked arousal (all p>0.2, see Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Statistical result with p-values.

claim: Post-stimulus gamma power increased linearly with rising pre-stimulus entropy (40–70 Hz, 0–400 ms; β = 0.04, SE = 0.01, p<0.001).
source: Third, we detected linearly increasing post-stimulus gamma power, representing early auditory evoked activity, with rising pre-stimulus entropy (40–70 Hz, 0–400 ms; β = 0.04, SE = 0.01, p<0.001, Figure 4c,f).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus figure references.

claim: Post-stimulus gamma power showed a tendency to decrease with growing pre-stimulus pupil size that did not reach statistical significance (β = −0.016, SE = 0.01, p=0.1).
source: Conversely, post-stimulus gamma power showed a tendency to decrease with growing pre-stimulus pupil size that did not reach statistical significance (β = −0.016, SE = 0.01, p=0.1; Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value.

claim: Auditory evoked gamma power was inversely influenced by desynchronization and arousal (ZWald = 3.6, p=0.0003).
source: Auditory evoked gamma power hence was inversely influenced by two different measures of brain state: while it increased with local cortical desynchronization, it decreased with growing arousal (ZWald = 3.6, p=0.0003).
evidence: Statistical comparison result with test statistic and p-value.

claim: Neither local desynchronization nor pupil size had any effect on the tone-evoked activity when expressed as event-related potentials.
source: Notably, neither local desynchronization nor pupil size had any effect on the tone-evoked activity when expressed as event-related potentials (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statement about null result with figure reference.

claim: Pre-stimulus entropy displayed a negative quadratic relationship with response criterion (log odds (log OR)=−0.06, SE = 0.02, p=0.02).
source: Participants were least biased and answered fastest at intermediate levels of pre-stimulus desynchronization: pre-stimulus entropy displayed a negative quadratic relationship with response criterion (log odds (log OR)=−0.06, SE = 0.02, p=0.02; Figure 5a, Supplementary file 10) and response speed (β = −0.012, SE = 0.004, p=0.002; Figure 5c, Supplementary file 12)
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus figure references.

claim: Pre-stimulus entropy displayed a negative quadratic relationship with response speed (β = −0.012, SE = 0.004, p=0.002).
source: Participants were least biased and answered fastest at intermediate levels of pre-stimulus desynchronization: pre-stimulus entropy displayed a negative quadratic relationship with response criterion (log odds (log OR)=−0.06, SE = 0.02, p=0.02; Figure 5a, Supplementary file 10) and response speed (β = −0.012, SE = 0.004, p=0.002; Figure 5c, Supplementary file 12)
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus figure references.

claim: Average predicted response times were lowest following intermediate pre-stimulus entropy (.716 s) compared to low (.762 s) and high (.786 s) entropy.
source: Average predicted response times were lowest following intermediate pre-stimulus entropy (.716 s) compared to low (.762 s) and high (.786 s) entropy.
evidence: Direct statement with predicted values from model.

claim: States of intermediate neural desynchronization led to a reduction in response time of 50–60 ms compared to high and low desynchronization states.
source: States of intermediate neural desynchronization hence led to a reduction in response time of 50–60 ms compared to high and low desynchronization states.
evidence: Direct statement about response time differences.

claim: Pupil size exhibited negative linear as well as quadratic relations with sensitivity (linear: log OR = −0.232, SE = 0.068, p=0.001; quadratic: log OR = −0.153, SE = −0.035, p<0.001).
source: Conversely, participants proved most sensitive at intermediate levels of arousal: pupil size exhibited negative linear as well as quadratic relations with sensitivity (linear: log OR = −0.232, SE = 0.068, p=0.001; quadratic: log OR = −0.153, SE = −0.035, p<0.001; Supplementary file 10) but not with response speed (β = −0.004, SE = 0.003, p=0.1; Figure 5d, Supplementary file 12).
evidence: Statistical results with effect sizes, standard errors, and p-values, plus figure references.

claim: Pupil size did not have a relationship with response speed (β = −0.004, SE = 0.003, p=0.1).
source: Conversely, participants proved most sensitive at intermediate levels of arousal: pupil size exhibited negative linear as well as quadratic relations with sensitivity (linear: log OR = −0.232, SE = 0.068, p=0.001; quadratic: log OR = −0.153, SE = −0.035, p<0.001; Supplementary file 10) but not with response speed (β = −0.004, SE = 0.003, p=0.1; Figure 5d, Supplementary file 12).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus figure references.

claim: Pupil size covaried with response criterion following a linearly decreasing relationship (log OR = −0.115, SE = 0.028, p<0.001).
source: Like pre-stimulus entropy, pupil size did covary with response criterion. However, the relationship was linearly decreasing (high arousal coincided with a decreased criterion; log OR = −0.115, SE = 0.028, p<0.001; Figure 5c) and lacked the marked quadratic relationship observed for pre-stimulus entropy (cf. Figure 5a).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value, plus figure references.

claim: Response criterion was predicted by EEG entropy following an inverted U shape but not by pupil size (ZWald = –2.9, p=0.004).
source: While response criterion was predicted by EEG entropy following an inverted U shape but not by pupil size (ZWald = –2.9, p=0.004), response speed was predominantly influenced by pre-stimulus entropy (ZWald = –1.94, p=0.05).
evidence: Statistical comparison result with test statistic and p-value.

claim: Response speed was predominantly influenced by pre-stimulus entropy (ZWald = –1.94, p=0.05).
source: While response criterion was predicted by EEG entropy following an inverted U shape but not by pupil size (ZWald = –2.9, p=0.004), response speed was predominantly influenced by pre-stimulus entropy (ZWald = –1.94, p=0.05).
evidence: Statistical comparison result with test statistic and p-value.

claim: Modelling decisions based on stimulus difficulty alone explained 56.4% of variance (conditional R2).
source: Of note, modelling decisions based on stimulus difficulty alone explained 56.4% of variance (conditional R2) while a model that additionally contained pre-stimulus EEG entropy and pupil size as predictors explained 63.2% of variance in behaviour.
evidence: Direct statement about model variance explained.

claim: A model that additionally contained pre-stimulus EEG entropy and pupil size as predictors explained 63.2% of variance in behaviour.
source: Of note, modelling decisions based on stimulus difficulty alone explained 56.4% of variance (conditional R2) while a model that additionally contained pre-stimulus EEG entropy and pupil size as predictors explained 63.2% of variance in behaviour.
evidence: Direct statement about model variance explained.

claim: Pre-stimulus oscillatory power was not significantly linked to behaviour (all p>0.15).
source: Oscillatory power however was not significantly linked to behaviour (all p>0.15) and including power as an additional predictor in the model of performance outlined above did not explain additional variance (model comparison; Bayes factor BFEntropy–Power = 98).
evidence: Statistical result with p-values and Bayes factor.

claim: Including power as an additional predictor in the model of performance did not explain additional variance (model comparison; Bayes factor BFEntropy–Power = 98).
source: Oscillatory power however was not significantly linked to behaviour (all p>0.15) and including power as an additional predictor in the model of performance outlined above did not explain additional variance (model comparison; Bayes factor BFEntropy–Power = 98).
evidence: Model comparison result with Bayes factor.

claim: Visual and auditory entropy were correlated (β = 0.40, SE = 0.009, p<0.001) but shared only 15% variance (R2 = 15%).
source: Unsurprisingly, as these spatial filter weights yield imperfect renderings of local cortical activity, we observed a sizable correlation between this visuo-occipital entropy signal and the auditory entropy signal central to our analyses (β = 0.40, SE = 0.009, p<0.001). However, since visual and auditory entropy were also sufficiently distinct (shared variance only R2 = 15%), more detailed analysed on their specific effects were warranted.
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, p-value, and variance explained.

claim: Visuo-occipital entropy signal showed a weak negative relationship with pupil size (β = −0.02, SE = 0.009, p=0.03).
source: We first regressed this visuo-occipital entropy signal on pupil size and observed a weak negative relationship (β = −0.02, SE = 0.009, p=0.03).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value.

claim: Visual cortex entropy was a markedly weaker predictor of single-trial phase coherence than auditory cortex entropy (model comparison; Bayes factor BFAuditory–Visual = 1416).
source: Adding to the domain specificity of our main findings, however, visual cortex entropy was a markedly weaker predictor of single-trial phase coherence (model comparison to a model with auditory entropy; Bayes factor BFAuditory–Visual = 1416), low-frequency power (BFAuditory–Visual = 1977), and gamma power (BFAuditory–Visual = 39 see Figure 6).
evidence: Model comparison result with Bayes factor and figure reference.

claim: Visual cortex entropy was a markedly weaker predictor of low-frequency power than auditory cortex entropy (BFAuditory–Visual = 1977).
source: Adding to the domain specificity of our main findings, however, visual cortex entropy was a markedly weaker predictor of single-trial phase coherence (model comparison to a model with auditory entropy; Bayes factor BFAuditory–Visual = 1416), low-frequency power (BFAuditory–Visual = 1977), and gamma power (BFAuditory–Visual = 39 see Figure 6).
evidence: Model comparison result with Bayes factor and figure reference.

claim: Visual cortex entropy was a markedly weaker predictor of gamma power than auditory cortex entropy (BFAuditory–Visual = 39).
source: Adding to the domain specificity of our main findings, however, visual cortex entropy was a markedly weaker predictor of single-trial phase coherence (model comparison to a model with auditory entropy; Bayes factor BFAuditory–Visual = 1416), low-frequency power (BFAuditory–Visual = 1977), and gamma power (BFAuditory–Visual = 39 see Figure 6).
evidence: Model comparison result with Bayes factor and figure reference.

claim: Visual cortex entropy did not exhibit any relationship with response criterion (log OR = 0.009, SE = 0.02, p=0.66).
source: Furthermore, visual cortex entropy did not exhibit any relationship with response criterion (log OR = 0.009, SE = 0.02, p=0.66; Supplementary file 11).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value.

claim: Visual cortex entropy had no effect on response speed (β = −0.002, SE = 0.003, p=0.50).
source: Visual cortex entropy also had no effect on response speed (β = −0.002, SE = 0.003, p=0.50).
evidence: Statistical result with effect size, standard error, and p-value.

claim: Auditory cortex entropy explained the response speed data better than visual cortex entropy (BFAuditory–Visual = 10.8).
source: Accordingly, auditory cortex entropy explained the response speed data better (BFAuditory–Visual = 10.8).
evidence: Model comparison result with Bayes factor.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal likely traces back to neuromodulatory activity and is associated with the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS).
source: The term arousal here and henceforth is used to refer to the general level of alertness which likely traces back to neuromodulatory activity and is associated with the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS).
evidence: Direct statement defining arousal based on established knowledge.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal captures locus coeruleus-norepinephrine activity (LC–NE).
source: Pupil-linked arousal, which captures locus coeruleus-norepinephrine activity (LC–NE; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016) has been shown to influence sensory evoked activity (McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) and the processing of task-relevant information (Murphy et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal has been shown to influence sensory evoked activity.
source: Pupil-linked arousal, which captures locus coeruleus-norepinephrine activity (LC–NE; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016) has been shown to influence sensory evoked activity (McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) and the processing of task-relevant information (Murphy et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal has been shown to influence the processing of task-relevant information.
source: Pupil-linked arousal, which captures locus coeruleus-norepinephrine activity (LC–NE; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016) has been shown to influence sensory evoked activity (McGinley et al., 2015a; McGinley et al., 2015b; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) and the processing of task-relevant information (Murphy et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Optimal performance at intermediate levels of arousal has reliably been observed.
source: Although optimal performance at intermediate levels of arousal has reliably been observed (Murphy et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015b; McGinley et al., 2015a; van den Brink et al., 2016; Faller et al., 2019), reports of linear effects on performance (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) or evoked activity (Neske and McCormick, 2018) in different tasks and species complicate this picture.
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Reports of linear effects of arousal on performance or evoked activity in different tasks and species complicate the picture of arousal-performance relationships.
source: Although optimal performance at intermediate levels of arousal has reliably been observed (Murphy et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015b; McGinley et al., 2015a; van den Brink et al., 2016; Faller et al., 2019), reports of linear effects on performance (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) or evoked activity (Neske and McCormick, 2018) in different tasks and species complicate this picture.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to contrasting findings.

claim: Relatively high neural desynchronization yielded improved encoding and representation of visual input in non-human animals.
source: In a separate line of experimental work in non-human animals, relatively high neural desynchronization yielded improved encoding and representation of visual (Goard and Dan, 2009; Pinto et al., 2013; Beaman et al., 2017) as well as auditory input (Marguet and Harris, 2011; Pachitariu et al., 2015; Sakata, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Relatively high neural desynchronization yielded improved encoding and representation of auditory input in non-human animals.
source: In a separate line of experimental work in non-human animals, relatively high neural desynchronization yielded improved encoding and representation of visual (Goard and Dan, 2009; Pinto et al., 2013; Beaman et al., 2017) as well as auditory input (Marguet and Harris, 2011; Pachitariu et al., 2015; Sakata, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Periods of desynchronization are characterized by reduced noise correlations in population activity.
source: Such periods of desynchronization are characterized by reduced noise correlations in population activity, and these patterns are commonly referred to as desynchronized cortical states.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about desynchronization.

claim: Desynchronized cortical states likely result from subtle changes in the balance of excitatory and inhibitory activity.
source: They likely result from subtle changes in the balance of excitatory and inhibitory activity (Renart et al., 2010; Haider et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: Behaviourally relevant changes in cortical desynchronization have been suggested to trace back to attention-related changes in thalamo-cortical interactions.
source: Notably, behaviourally relevant changes in cortical desynchronization have been suggested to trace back to attention-related changes in thalamo-cortical interactions (Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Desynchronization states can be expected to be of local nature and be limited to sensory cortical areas of the currently attended sensory domain.
source: Thus, such desynchronization states can be expected to be of local nature and be limited to sensory cortical areas of the currently attended sensory domain (Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited work.

claim: Local desynchronization and perceptual performance are positively linked in general.
source: Although local desynchronization and perceptual performance are positively linked in general (Beaman et al., 2017; Speed et al., 2019), the exact shape of their relationship (e.g., linear vs. quadratic) is unclear.
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: The exact shape of the relationship between local desynchronization and perceptual performance (e.g., linear vs. quadratic) is unclear.
source: Although local desynchronization and perceptual performance are positively linked in general (Beaman et al., 2017; Speed et al., 2019), the exact shape of their relationship (e.g., linear vs. quadratic) is unclear.
evidence: Statement about gap in knowledge despite cited evidence.

claim: Evidence for a similar mechanism of desynchronization affecting perception in humans has remained elusive.
source: Most notably, evidence for a similar mechanism in humans has remained elusive.
evidence: Statement about gap in knowledge.

claim: A tight link of pupil size and desynchronization has been claimed.
source: On the one hand, a tight link of pupil size and desynchronization has been claimed (McCormick, 1989; McCormick et al., 1991; McGinley et al., 2015a; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal and local cortical desynchronization have been found to be locally unrelated.
source: On the other hand, both measures have also been found to be locally unrelated (Beaman et al., 2017; Okun et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to contrasting findings.

claim: Varying noradrenergic and cholinergic activity could influence both local cortical activity and pupil size via afferent projections from brain-stem nuclei.
source: Varying noradrenergic and cholinergic activity could influence both, local cortical activity and the more global measure of pupil size via afferent projections from brain-stem nuclei (Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited work.

claim: EEG entropy as measured in the present data aligns closely with the spectral exponent, a previously suggested measure of E/I.
source: Also, EEG entropy as measured in the present data aligns closely with the spectral exponent, a previously suggested measure of E/I (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Gao et al., 2017; Waschke et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by figure and citations.

claim: EEG entropy calculated for a previously published data set aptly tracks changes in excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) cortical activity that occur under different anaesthetics.
source: Importantly, EEG entropy calculated for a previously published data set (Sarasso et al., 2015) aptly tracks changes in excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) cortical activity that occur under different anaesthetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statement supported by analysis of external dataset with citation and figure reference.

claim: Entropy of EEG signals is sensitive to the basic features of desynchronization (e.g. reduced oscillatory power).
source: Entropy of EEG signals thus is not only sensitive to the basic features of desynchronization (e.g. reduced oscillatory power) but also captures changes in a central underlying mechanism (E/I balance).
evidence: Statement based on inference from previous results.

claim: Entropy of EEG signals captures changes in E/I balance.
source: Entropy of EEG signals thus is not only sensitive to the basic features of desynchronization (e.g. reduced oscillatory power) but also captures changes in a central underlying mechanism (E/I balance).
evidence: Statement based on inference from previous results.

claim: A closed-loop set up allows for selective stimulation during specific states of brain activity while accounting for changes in the appearance of those states.
source: Such a closed-loop set up allows for selective stimulation during specific states of brain activity while accounting for changes in the appearance of those states and hence represents a powerful tool with a multitude of potential applications in research but also therapy (Sitaram et al., 2017; Ezzyat et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about methodology with citations to applications.

claim: Local cortical desynchronization and pupil-linked arousal were weakly positively correlated.
source: Although local cortical desynchronization and pupil-linked arousal were weakly positively correlated, both did not only shape the ongoing EEG activity into distinct states, but also differentially influenced sensory processing at the level of single trials
evidence: Summary statement of main findings.

claim: Phase-locked activity in low frequencies over auditory cortices was highest following intermediate levels of pre-stimulus desynchronization.
source: On the one hand, phase-locked activity in low frequencies as well as stimulus-related gamma power over auditory cortices was highest following intermediate levels of pre-stimulus desynchronization.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings.

claim: Stimulus-related gamma power over auditory cortices was highest following intermediate levels of pre-stimulus desynchronization.
source: On the one hand, phase-locked activity in low frequencies as well as stimulus-related gamma power over auditory cortices was highest following intermediate levels of pre-stimulus desynchronization.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings.

claim: Low-frequency power during and after a stimulus increased linearly with pre-stimulus arousal.
source: On the other hand, low-frequency power during and after a stimulus increased linearly with pre-stimulus arousal.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings.

claim: Response criterion and speed exhibited an inverted u-shaped relationship with local cortical desynchronization, where intermediate desynchronization corresponded to minimal response bias and fastest responses.
source: Response criterion and speed exhibited an inverted u-shaped relationship with local cortical desynchronization, where intermediate desynchronization corresponded to minimal response bias and fastest responses.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings.

claim: An analogous relationship was found for arousal and sensitivity, revealing highest sensitivity at intermediate arousal levels.
source: An analogous relationship was found for arousal and sensitivity, revealing highest sensitivity at intermediate arousal levels.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings.

claim: Fluctuations in arousal are likely realized by afferent cholinergic and noradrenergic projections into sensory cortical areas.
source: While fluctuations in arousal are likely realized by afferent cholinergic and noradrenergic projections into sensory cortical areas (Robbins, 1997; Carter et al., 2010), desynchronization states might result from efferent feedback connections (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Zagha et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited literature.

claim: Desynchronization states might result from efferent feedback connections.
source: While fluctuations in arousal are likely realized by afferent cholinergic and noradrenergic projections into sensory cortical areas (Robbins, 1997; Carter et al., 2010), desynchronization states might result from efferent feedback connections (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Zagha et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited literature.

claim: Global arousal states and local desynchronization states jointly influence sensory processing and performance.
source: Our results speak to a model in which global arousal states and local desynchronization states jointly influence sensory processing and performance.
evidence: Summary interpretation of findings.

claim: Participants compared each tone to an implicit standard, the median (=mean) pitch of the set.
source: On each trial participants were presented with one tone, taken from a set of seven pure tones (increasing pitch from tone 1 through tone 7), and had to decide whether that tone was rather high or low in pitch with regard to the overall set of tones. Participants thus compared each tone to an implicit standard, the median (=mean) pitch of the set.
evidence: Direct statement about task design.

claim: The task yielded in all participants a valid psychometric function mapping stimulus pitch to perceptual decisions.
source: This yielded in all participants a valid psychometric function mapping stimulus pitch to perceptual decisions (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statement about task validity with figure reference.

claim: Desynchronized cortical states have previously been associated in the rodent with enhanced encoding of auditory stimuli.
source: Desynchronized cortical states have previously been associated in the rodent with enhanced encoding of auditory stimuli (Marguet and Harris, 2011), more reliable neural responses (Pachitariu et al., 2015), and improved perceptual performance (Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Desynchronized cortical states have previously been associated in the rodent with more reliable neural responses.
source: Desynchronized cortical states have previously been associated in the rodent with enhanced encoding of auditory stimuli (Marguet and Harris, 2011), more reliable neural responses (Pachitariu et al., 2015), and improved perceptual performance (Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Desynchronized cortical states have previously been associated in the rodent with improved perceptual performance.
source: Desynchronized cortical states have previously been associated in the rodent with enhanced encoding of auditory stimuli (Marguet and Harris, 2011), more reliable neural responses (Pachitariu et al., 2015), and improved perceptual performance (Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: When optogenetically inducing synchronization, perception is impaired.
source: Instead, when optogenetically inducing synchronization, perception is impaired (Nandy et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Arousal has been linked to increased sensory processing of visual stimuli in mice and humans.
source: Conversely, arousal been linked to increased sensory processing of visual stimuli in mice (Neske and McCormick, 2018) and humans (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: Perceptual performance was found to be highest at either intermediate or maximum arousal levels.
source: However, perceptual performance was found to be highest at either intermediate (McGinley et al., 2015a; Neske and McCormick, 2018) or maximum arousal levels (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to contrasting findings.

claim: Pre-stimulus alpha power prior to stimulus onset has been tightly linked to changes in response criterion and confidence.
source: More specifically, however, alpha power (8–12 Hz) prior to stimulus onset has been tightly linked to changes in response criterion and confidence (Iemi et al., 2017; Samaha et al., 2017; Wöstmann et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: Pre-stimulus alpha power is hypothesized to represent changes in baseline excitability, linking it to response criterion following an inverted u-shaped relationship.
source: Pre-stimulus alpha power is hypothesized to represent changes in baseline excitability, linking it to response criterion following an inverted u-shaped relationship (Rajagovindan and Ding, 2011; Kloosterman et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The relationship of desynchronization and response criterion might trace back to task- and attention-specific input to sensory cortical regions via efferent projections leading to a change in net inhibition.
source: These previous findings and the here reported connection of desynchronization and response criterion might at least partially trace back to the same underlying mechanism: that is, task- and attention-specific input to sensory cortical regions via efferent projections leading to a change in net inhibition.
evidence: Speculative statement connecting findings to mechanism.

claim: EEG entropy potentially poses a more sensitive proxy of underlying neural processes than oscillatory power.
source: Thus, EEG entropy potentially poses a more sensitive proxy of underlying neural processes than oscillatory power and explains more behavioural variance.
evidence: Speculative statement based on inference from results.

claim: Desynchronization and arousal might interact separately with the two building blocks of sensory evoked responses: phase resetting of low-frequency oscillations and additive low-frequency activity.
source: Effectively, desynchronization and arousal might interact separately with the two, long-debated building blocks of sensory evoked responses: phase resetting of low-frequency oscillations and additive low-frequency activity (Shah, 2004; Sauseng et al., 2007).
evidence: Speculative statement with citations to relevant concepts.

claim: Tones presented into states of intermediate desynchronization led to a stronger phase-reset.
source: Tones presented into states of intermediate desynchronization thus led to a stronger phase-reset.
evidence: Interpretation of findings.

claim: The parallel in neural and behavioural results cautiously suggests a change in the precision of representations that depends on the current desynchronization state.
source: This striking parallel in neural and behavioural results cautiously suggests a change in the precision of representations that depends on the current desynchronization state.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings.

claim: Intermediate arousal might optimize the integration of sensory representation into an existing reference frame.
source: Second, the impact of arousal on post-stimulus alpha power and perceptual sensitivity, in the light of earlier interpretations (Voigt et al., 2018) proposes a similar mechanism: in addition to a clearer early representation of sensory information, intermediate arousal might optimize the integration of such a representation into an existing reference frame.
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citation.

claim: Integration of sensory representations likely involves cortico-cortical feedback connections and is essential to allow sensitive perceptual decisions.
source: This integration likely involves cortico-cortical feedback connections (Tallon-Baudry, 1999) and is essential to allow sensitive perceptual decisions.
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited work.

claim: States of high arousal could lead to over-amplification of responses and prove detrimental to sensory encoding and perception.
source: States of high arousal could thus in principle lead to a similar process of over-amplification and hence prove detrimental to sensory encoding and perception.
evidence: Speculative statement based on inference from previous findings.

claim: Relatively highest levels of responsiveness in auditory cortical neurons overall can entail the loss of response specificity crucial for precise encoding and perception.
source: First, relatively highest levels of responsiveness in auditory cortical neurons overall can entail the loss of response specificity crucial for precise encoding and perception (Otazu et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Over-amplified responses to auditory stimuli have been linked to age-related decreases of cortical inhibition.
source: Second, and in line with this rationale, over-amplified responses to auditory stimuli have been linked to age-related decreases of cortical inhibition (Herrmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Noradrenergic projections might transmit task-related activity most efficiently at intermediate arousal levels.
source: Third, a recent experiment researching the impact of arousal on visual processing in mice yielded a highly similar pattern of results (Neske and McCormick, 2018). Neske and McCormick (2018) highlight the role of noradrenergic projections which might transmit task-related activity most efficiently at intermediate arousal levels (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005).
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited work.

claim: Arousal shapes global brain states via afferent noradrenergic projections and predominantly influences sensitivity.
source: The data are commensurate with a model where, on the one hand, arousal shapes global brain states via afferent noradrenergic projections and predominantly influences sensitivity.
evidence: Summary interpretation of findings as a model.

claim: Local cortical desynchronization in task-related sensory areas generates local states via attention-dependent feedback connections and impacts response criterion and speed.
source: Conversely, we see local cortical desynchronization in task-related sensory areas to generate local states via attention-dependent feedback connections and to impact response criterion and speed.
evidence: Summary interpretation of findings as a model.

claim: The shared variability of neuronal populations and its impact on the responses of single neurons are shaped by an additive and a multiplicative source of variation in neural gain.
source: It has been suggested that the shared variability of neuronal populations and its impact on the responses of single neurons are shaped by an additive and a multiplicative source of variation in neural gain (Arieli et al., 1996; Scholvinck et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: Instantaneous fluctuations of cortical activity, or local cortical desynchronization, are believed to have an additive effect on evoked responses.
source: Instantaneous fluctuations of cortical activity, or local cortical desynchronization, are believed to have an additive effect on evoked responses (Arieli et al., 1996).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Arousal-related LC–NE activity exerts a multiplicative influence on the tuning of sensory neurons, which has been suggested to entail relatively sharper tuning curves.
source: Furthermore, arousal-related LC–NE activity exerts a multiplicative influence on the tuning of sensory neurons, which has been suggested to entail relatively sharper tuning curves (Mather et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Recent findings challenge the view that arousal sharpens tuning curves by showing pupil-linked arousal-related broadening of sensory neural tuning curves.
source: However, recent findings challenge this view by showing pupil-linked arousal-related broadening of sensory neural tuning curves (Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to contrasting finding.

claim: It is unlikely that either additive or multiplicative factors alone are the sole source of variability in stimulus-related activity and behaviour.
source: Additionally, it is unlikely that either additive or multiplicative factors alone are the sole source of variability in stimulus-related activity and behaviour (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: The present data allow the testable prediction that selective attention and desynchronization primarily exert an additive influence on neural gain, while LC–NE activity and arousal impact neural gain in a multiplicative fashion.
source: However, the present data allow the testable prediction that selective attention and desynchronization primarily exert an additive influence on neural gain, while LC–NE activity and arousal impact neural gain in a multiplicative fashion.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on interpretation of findings.

claim: LC–NE activity has been proposed to reflect changes in arousal captured by variations in pupil size.
source: LC–NE activity has been proposed to reflect changes in arousal captured by variations in pupil size (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Fluctuations in pupil size have been linked to activity in the superior colliculus.
source: Although fluctuations in pupil size have recently been linked to activity in the superior colliculus (Wang et al., 2012) or the ventral tegmental area (de Gee et al., 2017) and also carry information about cholinergic activity (Reimer et al., 2016), converging evidence suggests a tight connection to LC–NE activity (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016; de Gee et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Glutamatergic cortico-cortical and thalamo-cortical feedback connections have been proposed as a source of varying states of desynchronization.
source: At the same time, in addition to adrenergic and cholinergic projections from brain-stem nuclei, glutamatergic cortico-cortical and thalamo-cortical feedback connections have been proposed as a source of varying states of desynchronization (Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: The widespread NE projections from LC are a likely cause for the demonstrable effects of NE-linked arousal on sensory encoding in both the auditory as well as visual domain.
source: The widespread NE projections from LC (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005) are a likely cause for the demonstrable effects of NE-linked arousal on sensory encoding in both the auditory (McGinley et al., 2015a) as well as visual domain (Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited work.

claim: Arousal states should not differ substantially between different sensory cortical regions based on widespread NE projections.
source: The widespread NE projections from LC (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005) are a likely cause for the demonstrable effects of NE-linked arousal on sensory encoding in both the auditory (McGinley et al., 2015a) as well as visual domain (Vinck et al., 2015). This rationale would thus predict that arousal states should not differ substantially between different sensory cortical regions.
evidence: Prediction based on inference from cited work.

claim: Modulatory effects of arousal have been found to depend on the experimental context as well as on the sensory modality.
source: However, modulatory effects of arousal have been found to depend on the experimental context as well as on the sensory modality (Pakan et al., 2016; Shimaoka et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: The weak correlation of desynchronization and arousal might trace back to the focus on auditory cortical areas.
source: The weak correlation of desynchronization and arousal might thus trace back to our focus on auditory cortical areas.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings.

claim: The overall level of arousal should have widespread but modality- and context-specific impact on sensory processing and behaviour.
source: While the overall level of arousal should have widespread but modality- and context-specific impact on sensory processing and behaviour (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGinley et al., 2015b), the desynchronization of local sensory neural populations could be largely unrelated to, and take place on top of, those global changes (Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited work.

claim: The desynchronization of local sensory neural populations could be largely unrelated to, and take place on top of, global arousal changes.
source: While the overall level of arousal should have widespread but modality- and context-specific impact on sensory processing and behaviour (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGinley et al., 2015b), the desynchronization of local sensory neural populations could be largely unrelated to, and take place on top of, those global changes (Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited work.

claim: Local and modality-specific changes in desynchronization have been assumed to arise from both thalamo- and cortico-cortical feedback connections that represent the allocation of selective attention.
source: Such rather local and modality-specific changes in desynchronization have been assumed to arise from both thalamo- and cortico-cortical feedback connections that represent the allocation of selective attention (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Zagha et al., 2013; Zagha and McCormick, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: Glutamatergic projections between thalamus, prefrontal, and sensory cortical areas might shape the local net degree of inhibition in populations of sensory neurons via AMPA and NMDA receptors.
source: More precisely, glutamatergic projections between thalamus, prefrontal, and sensory cortical areas might shape the local net degree of inhibition in populations of sensory neurons via AMPA and NMDA receptors and hence influence time-varying local desynchronization.
evidence: Speculative mechanistic statement.

claim: Contingent on the specific task structure, selective attention increases desynchronization in neurons with stimulus-related receptive fields but also across a broader range of task-relevant neurons.
source: In fact, contingent on the specific task structure, selective attention increases desynchronization in neurons with stimulus-related receptive fields but also across a broader range of task-relevant neurons (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: Noradrenergic and cholinergic neuromodulation have been suggested as a candidate mechanism underlying dynamics in E/I balance.
source: Noradrenergic and cholinergic neuromodulation however, have been suggested as a candidate mechanism underlying such dynamics (Froemke, 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: The involvement of two partially related mechanisms in the concomitant generation of desynchronization and arousal states appears likely.
source: All things considered, the involvement of two partially related mechanisms in the concomitant generation of desynchronization and arousal states appears likely.
evidence: Summary inference from discussion.

claim: Desynchronization states presumably are shaped by feedback connections that could result from fluctuations in selective attention.
source: On the one hand, desynchronization states presumably are shaped by feedback connections that could result from fluctuations in selective attention (Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: Speculative statement with citation.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal states at least partially hinge on varying levels of LC–NE activity which are propagated via vast projections towards most regions of cortex.
source: On the other hand, pupil-linked arousal states at least partially hinge on varying levels of LC–NE activity (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016) which are propagated via vast projections towards most regions of cortex and which might be related to overall changes in the availability of cognitive resources.
evidence: Statement based on inference from cited work.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal might be related to overall changes in the availability of cognitive resources.
source: On the other hand, pupil-linked arousal states at least partially hinge on varying levels of LC–NE activity (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016) which are propagated via vast projections towards most regions of cortex and which might be related to overall changes in the availability of cognitive resources.
evidence: Speculative statement.

claim: Technical advances have promoted the use of closed-loop paradigms to various areas of neuroscientific research, where the main application lies in neurofeedback.
source: Technical advances have promoted the use of such closed-loop paradigms to various areas of neuroscientific research, where the main application lies in neurofeedback.
evidence: Statement about methodological developments.

claim: Neurofeedback tries to modify behaviour by providing participants with sensory information that is directly proportional to their current brain state.
source: Neurofeedback tries to modify behaviour by providing participants with sensory information that is directly proportional to their current brain state (Sitaram et al., 2017; Faller et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about neurofeedback with citations.

claim: Recent studies have used closed-loop approaches to relate fluctuations in working memory or decision making to brain activity in real-time.
source: Just recently, a number of methodically sophisticated studies have used the power of this approach to relate fluctuations in working memory (Ezzyat et al., 2018) or decision making (Peixoto et al., 2019) to brain activity in real-time.
evidence: Statement about recent applications with citations.

claim: Fast fluctuations in neural activity have been suggested to depict synaptic activity and potentially trace back to thalamo- or cortico-cortical interactions.
source: On the one hand, fast fluctuations have been suggested to depict synaptic activity and potentially trace back to thalamo- or cortico-cortical interactions (Haider and McCormick, 2009; Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: Slow fluctuations in neural activity potentially depict the influence of arousal or neuromodulatory activity in general.
source: On the other hand, slow fluctuations potentially depict the influence of arousal or neuromodulatory activity in general (Okun et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: States of local desynchronization likely operate on short time scales in the range of several hundred milliseconds.
source: While states of local desynchronization likely operate on short time scales in the range of several hundred milliseconds, pupil-linked arousal states rather stretch across several seconds.
evidence: Inference from autocorrelation analysis.

claim: Pupil-linked arousal states stretch across several seconds.
source: While states of local desynchronization likely operate on short time scales in the range of several hundred milliseconds, pupil-linked arousal states rather stretch across several seconds.
evidence: Inference from autocorrelation analysis.

claim: The strong negative relationship of desynchronization with low-frequency power replicates previous findings and is tightly linked to the concept of entropy.
source: The strong negative relationship with low-frequency power replicates previous findings and is tightly linked to the concept of entropy (Waschke et al., 2017).
